tlstractor

The R package tlstractor implements TLS-Tractor (Transfer Learning of Summary Statistics to Tractor), a transfer-learning framework for improving the power of local ancestry-aware genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in admixed populations. TLS-Tractor combines internal individual-level admixed-cohort data with external standard GWAS summary statistics to improve ancestry-specific effect estimation and overall association testing.

Tractor is a local ancestry-aware GWAS method that estimates ancestry-specific genetic effects and provides an overall test of genetic association, but its power is limited by the sample size of available admixed cohorts. Standard GWAS summary statistics are available at a much larger scale, but they cannot be directly incorporated into Tractor because the model parameterization differs. TLS-Tractor bridges this gap by transferring information from external standard GWAS summary statistics into the Tractor framework.

Core computational steps are implemented in C++ for efficient analysis of large datasets. See Key assumptions before applying the method.

Installation

tlstractor requires R 4.5.0 or later.

For Conda users only

If you are not using Conda, skip this subsection and continue to the installation options below.

To install tlstractor in a dedicated Conda environment, run:

conda create -n r-tlstractor -c conda-forge r-base -y
conda activate r-tlstractor
conda install -c conda-forge compilers make pkg-config zlib -y

Install tlstractor

Option 1: Install the development version from GitHub

Use this option to install the current development version.

install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("Wenxuan-Lu/tlstractor")

Option 2: Install a specific release

Use this option to install a fixed, reproducible release. Replace v0.1.0 with the desired release tag.

install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("Wenxuan-Lu/tlstractor@v0.1.0")

If installation fails, see Installation troubleshooting.

Quick start

This package implements a three-step workflow that is fully compatible with Tractor scripts but substantially faster. The three steps are: extracts local ancestry tracts, harmonizes external standard GWAS summary statistics, and runs TLS-Tractor.

The example below is a minimal runnable template. File names and column names are illustrative. Please adapt them to your own data. For a complete pipeline walkthrough, see the TLS-Tractor tutorial.

Required inputs

Individual-level data from the main study / internal cohort:

  • Phased genotypes with local ancestry inference results, provided in one of the following formats:

    • For RFMix2/Gnomix local ancestry inference:

      • cohort.vcf(.gz): phased genotypes, with GT encoded as phased calls such as 0|1

      • cohort.msp.tsv(.gz): local ancestry labels

    • For FLARE local ancestry inference:

      • cohort.vcf(.gz): FLARE output VCF containing both phased genotypes and local ancestry labels

  • Phenotype file: pheno.txt with columns id and pheno

  • Optional covariate file: covariates.txt with columns such as id, cov1, cov2, and cov3

Summary-level data from the external cohort:

  • External standard GWAS summary statistics: external_sumstats.txt with columns CHR, POS, ID, REF, ALT, BETA, SE, and optional columns N, AF, N_CASE, N_CONTROL, AF_CASE, and AF_CONTROL.

Minimal example 

library(tlstractor)

# 1) Extract tracts (choose one option)

# Option A: phased VCF + MSP file from RFMix2/Gnomix
extract_tracts(
  vcf_path = "cohort.vcf.gz",
  msp_path = "cohort.msp.tsv",
  num_ancs = 2L,
  output_formats = "gds"
)

# Option B: FLARE VCF
# extract_tracts_flare(
#   vcf_path = "cohort.vcf.gz",
#   num_ancs = 2L,
#   output_formats = "gds"
# )

# 2) Harmonize external standard GWAS summary statistics
munge_sumstats(
  gds_path = "cohort.gds",
  sumstats_path = "external_sumstats.txt",
  match_by = "CHR-POS",
  output_path = "external_sumstats_munged.txt"
)

# 3) Run TLS-Tractor
tlstractor(
  gds_path = "cohort.gds",
  sumstats_path = "external_sumstats_munged.txt",
  method = "linear", # use "logistic" for binary traits
  cond_local = TRUE, # whether to condition on local ancestry terms
  pheno_path = "pheno.txt",
  pheno_id_col = "id",
  pheno_col = "pheno",
  covar_path = "covariates.txt",
  covar_id_col = "id",
  covar_cols = c("cov1", "cov2", "cov3"),
  output_prefix = "tlstractor",
  n_cores = 4L
)

Main outputs

  1. Tracts GDS (cohort.gds) — HDF5-based GDS file containing:

    • sample.id — sample identifiers
    • snp.chromosome, snp.position, snp.id, snp.ref, snp.alt — variant metadata
    • dosage/anc0..ancK, hapcount/anc0..ancK — ancestry-specific alternative-allele dosage (0, 1, 2) and local ancestry haplotype count (0, 1, 2) matrices

  2. Munged summary statistics (external_sumstats_munged.txt) — tab-delimited file with columns:

    • CHR, POS, ID, REF, ALT — variant information
    • BETA, SE — effect size and standard error
    • Optional columns (when provided): N, AF, N_CASE, N_CONTROL, AF_CASE, AF_CONTROL — allele frequencies and sample sizes
    • GDS_ID — internal variant index linking the summary statistics to the GDS file

  3. TLS-Tractor results (tlstractor.txt.gz) — gzip-compressed tab-delimited file with columns:

    Variant metadata and internal-cohort summaries

    • CHROM, POS, ID, REF, ALT — variant information
    • main_N — number of internal-cohort samples analyzed
    • main_N_case, main_N_control — number of internal-cohort cases and controls (logistic analysis only)
    • AF — overall allele frequency
    • AF_anc* — ancestry-specific allele frequencies (e.g., AF_anc0, AF_anc1 for two-way admixture)
    • AF_case_anc*, AF_control_anc* — ancestry-specific allele frequencies in cases and controls (logistic analysis only)
    • LAprop_anc* — local ancestry proportions at the variant
    • LAprop_case_anc*, LAprop_control_anc* — local ancestry proportions in cases and controls (logistic analysis only)

    Analysis metadata

    • has_sumstats — logical indicator (TRUE/FALSE) of whether external summary statistics were available for the variant. When FALSE, the variant was analyzed using internal data alone.
    • fallback_used — logical indicator (TRUE/FALSE) of whether QR decomposition fallback was used during computation. When TRUE, results may have reduced numerical stability and should be interpreted cautiously.

    Association results

    • joint_pval — joint p-value testing all ancestry-specific SNP dosage effects
    • beta_anc* — ancestry-specific effect estimates (linear coefficients for continuous traits and log odds ratios for binary traits)
    • se_anc* — standard errors of ancestry-specific effects
    • pval_anc* — p-values for ancestry-specific effects

    Local ancestry effects (only present when cond_local=TRUE)

    • LAeff_anc* — local ancestry effect estimates
    • LAse_anc* — standard errors of local ancestry effects
    • LApval_anc* — p-values for local ancestry effect

Key assumptions

TLS-Tractor relies on three core assumptions:

  1. Unrelated individuals in the internal cohort.

  2. No sample overlap between internal and external cohorts.

  3. Comparable admixture profiles across internal and external cohorts.

    TLS-Tractor relies on a transportability assumption equivalent to fixed-effect GWAS meta-analysis: after appropriate covariate adjustment, the standard GWAS effect that would be estimated in the internal cohort and the standard GWAS effect estimated in the external cohort target the same underlying genetic effect, with observed differences arising from sampling variation rather than true heterogeneity. In practice, this requires comparable admixture profiles across cohorts, including the same ancestral components and similar global ancestry proportions.

In addition, common GWAS meta-analysis considerations still apply. For example, the internal and external datasets should have compatible allele coding, genome build, trait definition, phenotype curation, sample inclusion criteria, and covariate adjustment.

The package tutorial provides recommended checks for these assumptions and guidance on interpreting diagnostic results.

Common usage notes

1. File formats for tract extraction

For tract extraction, tlstractor can output three formats: the original Tractor text format (.txt or .txt.gz), ancestry-specific VCF files (.vcf or .vcf.gz), and a compact GDS format (.gds).

GDS is the native input format for TLS-Tractor association analysis. It stores ancestry-specific allele dosages and local ancestry haplotype counts in a single file, reducing storage and simplifying downstream analysis compared with the multiple text files used by standard Tractor workflows.

The tract-extraction step in tlstractor can therefore be used as a drop-in replacement for existing Tractor workflows. In our tests, the C++ implementation is at least 35 times faster than the original Tractor tract-extraction scripts.

If you already have tracts extracted in Tractor-style text format, you do not need to re-extract them. You can convert them directly to GDS format using convert_txt_to_gds(). Similarly, GDS files can be converted back to Tractor-style text format using convert_gds_to_txt().

2. Running Tractor with tlstractor

In addition to TLS-Tractor analysis, tlstractor can fit the Tractor model using internal individual-level data. The C++ implementation provides substantially shorter runtime and lower memory usage. See ?tlstractor for details.

3. Setting the number of cores

tlstractor() supports multi-core computation. By default, the package attempts to detect the number of available cores and avoid using more cores than appropriate for the current computing environment. If core detection does not work as expected, you can manually override the detected number of available cores:

# For example, set the number of available cores to 4.
options(
  parallelly.availableCores.custom = function() 4L,
  parallelly.availableCores.methods = "custom"
)

On shared clusters, make sure this number does not exceed the number of cores requested from the scheduler.

Installation troubleshooting

Read this section only if installation fails.

1. Check R/Bioconductor dependencies

If installation fails while installing or loading gdsfmt, install it explicitly from Bioconductor:

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("gdsfmt")

Then retry installing tlstractor.

2. Check system build requirements

tlstractor contains C++ code and links against zlib. Installation may fail if compilers, make, pkg-config, or the zlib development files are missing.

Quick check

Run Sys.which(c("make", "g++", "pkg-config")) in R. make and g++ should be non-empty. pkg-config is recommended because it helps the installer locate zlib, but installation may still succeed without it if zlib is available in standard compiler/linker paths.

To check whether zlib is visible through pkg-config, run system("pkg-config --exists zlib") == 0 in R. This should return TRUE. If pkg-config is not installed, skip the zlib check and install the required tools below.

Install required tools

  • Windows: install Rtools matching your R version.
  • macOS: run xcode-select --install, then install zlib and pkg-config, for example with brew install zlib pkg-config.
  • Debian/Ubuntu: run sudo apt-get install -y build-essential zlib1g-dev pkg-config.
  • Fedora/RHEL/CentOS: run sudo dnf install -y gcc gcc-c++ make zlib-devel pkgconf-pkg-config.
  • Alpine: run apk add --no-cache build-base zlib-dev pkgconf.

Then retry installing tlstractor.

Advanced: manual zlib configuration

This is only needed if installation still fails after zlib has been installed.

Set zlib paths explicitly, replacing the example paths with the locations on your system:

Sys.setenv(
  ZLIB_CPPFLAGS = "-I/path/to/include",
  ZLIB_LIBS = "-L/path/to/lib -lz"
)

Then retry installation.

Citation

The TLS-Tractor manuscript is in preparation. A formal citation will be added after the preprint or paper is available.

TLS-Tractor extends the Tractor framework, so please also cite the original Tractor paper:

Atkinson, E.G., Maihofer, A.X., Kanai, M. et al. Tractor uses local ancestry to enable the inclusion of admixed individuals in GWAS and to boost power. Nature Genetics 53, 195–204 (2021). Link
